subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The $350,000,000 of capital
invested, I should judge, consists not entirely of moneys expended on assets for the National Railways, but expended in many ways to wipe out deficits of former years-which are losses, of course.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: No, but capital investments exactly similar to this the hon. member says do not affect the debt. If that is correct, all these non-active assets so invested should now be deducted from the national debt, indeed, should never have been added to it.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not contending that the debt has not increased, but I am contending that an increase on the debt if you have a corresponding asset, an asset in this case that will directly influence the earning power of the National Railways, cannot be considered as affecting the surplus one way or the other.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Whether it pays interest or not? Does the hon. member say all the other mortgages taken from the National Railways which do not bear interest should now be deducted from the national debt, seeing they were added before?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I am not going to be misled into saying something I did not start out to say. What I say is this: If the moneys expended for the purpose of betterments on the Canadian National railways, and those having a direct effect upon their earning power, were spent for that purpose, then the surplus 
for the year is not affected thereby. I take it a surplus means, in the ordinary acceptation of the term in business, the excess of revenues, in this ease taxation and perhaps other sources of revenue, over ordinary expenditures for the year; in other words, it is known as a profit in business; we perhaps do not speak of it in that way in connection with the national finances. That is my contention, that the creation of a debt, if a corresponding asset is thereby established, does not affect the surplus for the year.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There is some use talking with the hon. member, and therefore I embrace the opportunity. If we build a post office it enables the Post Office department the better to earn their revenue, probably to earn more. It is an asset that we possess, does the hon. member argue that the cost of that should not be part of our national debt?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The hon. member misunderstood me entirely. I am not arguing about the debt. There is no question that the debt has been increased, but I say the government has a right to make a statement at the end of the year of the moneys which have been expended for services and which will never come back, and set against that the amount received by way of taxes or from other similar sources; and if there is an excess of receipts over expenditures there is a real surplus by the amount of which the debt can be reduced, and if the excess is the other way there is a deficit. That is my understanding of accountancy. I shall be very glad to argue the point with my hon. friend on another occasion.
So, Mr. Speaker, I sincerely congratulate the government on its surplus. Possibly the leader of the opposition will contest that when he speaks next week. I congratulate the government on the improved financial position of the country, and not least on the improved condition of the National railways.
But when I say that, Mr. Speaker, I want also to add that in my view the budget has certain serious defects, certain errors of omission, and of commission as well. I regret, in the first place, that the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has not seen fit to abolish those taxes that are sometimes, and so appropriately, called . the nuisance taxes. From the outset of their imposition under the former government I have opposed the stamp taxes upon commercial paper, and more latterly upon receipts as well. I have never been able to see that a tax so irritating in its nature, and one that is not based upon any logical principle, should have been imposed upon the people of Canada. Further, when the

The Budget-Mr. Euler
taxes for the ensuing year were being reduced by the removal of the sales tax in certain instances, I should have been glad if the government had at the same time considered the reduction of postage from three to two cents, believing it would not only be in the national interest, but that it would not have reduced the revenues in any degree whatever.
I regret also we have had no pronouncement, except perhaps with regard to one small item, with regard to the income tax. I should like to see some modification and some simplification of the income tax. I was more disappointed with regard to one thing perhaps than with regard to anything else, and that is that we have had no announcement from the government with regard to the creation of what is sometimes known as a tariff commission, and without the knowledge that only such a commission can give we have had some haphazard reductions in the tariff.
I regret further that we have had no legislation proposed for the relief of Canadian industry because of the depreciated currency of foreign countries with which we are in competition. It may be the government foresees the day at no distant date when these foreign countries, England and possibly continental nations, as a result of the Dawes' report, may go upon the gold standard basis and in that way the matter may correct itself; but we still have the condition under which industry in Canada is labouring because of the lower wage situation in countries which are now in strong competition with Canada. The other evening the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) made some comment with regard to the Canadian manufacturer of boots and shoes. That hon. gentleman is very-fair in debate, and I am quite sure he did not intend to be unfair in this case. During mv remarks in the debate on the motion for the adoption of the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, I had made some statement with regard to the difficulties experienced by the Canadian shoe manufacturer on account of the importation of British boots and shoes. The tariff on British boots and shoes by reason of the preferential arrangement is not 30 per cent but is now 16f per cent. That, coupled with the depreciated rate of exchange, and the lower labour costs in England, constitute the strongest competition that the Canadian shoe manufacturer has to contend with. But my hon. friend referred almost entirely to competition in that line with the United States manufacturer and stated-I do not desire to quote him incorrectly-that the tariff on American boots and shoes ought to be sufficient, and further hinted, or stated very broadly, that he
thought the difficulties of the Canadian shoe manufacturer were largely the result of inefficiency in his factories, and also arose from the fact that those factories had to carry a very large amount of watered stock.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I desire to contradict that
statement. There may be a few shoe factories in Canada where the matter of watered stock probably led to their going into liquidation. But in the riding from which I come there are ten or twelve shoe industries, and I want to say for the benefit of the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Garland) that in those concerns there is no watered stock, nor are they inefficiently conducted. It might interest the House to know that some four years ago the shoe industries of Canada exported to twenty-eight foreign countries in the year goods valued at approximately 85,500,000. Since that time tariffs have been raised in these foreign countries, exchange has depreciated, labour costs have gone down, so that last year-or rather the year ending in February last-the exports of boots and shoes from Canada to foreign countries had sunk to less than 8300,000.
With regard to the preferential tariff I should like to say, as I said on a previous occasion, that we ought to give consideration to Canada first; and that under present conditions of exchange and cheap labour the preference ought to be withdrawn or materially reduced. The present situation, as the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) said, is a one-sided arrangement. If we acted entirely on a business basis with regard to the tariff no one could say that our friends in Britain could find any fault with that attitude because they are pursuing that course themselves. I think I mentioned on a previous occasion that that was very well proven by their attitude with regard to the embargo on Canadian cattle which was a protective measure purely and simply, although another reason was given. Then we had later a rejection by the British people of the proposed Imperial preference arrangement that was enunciated by right hon. Mr. Baldwin at the last Imperial conference in London when the Prime Minister of Canada was present. And within less than two weeks we have had another instance of the attitude of the British government, in that they have removed the preference that Canada enjoyed in the British market as compared with the United States. So it seems to me the government might very fairly' and very logically consider some sort of modification of the preference.
The Budget-Mr. Elder

I do not intend to speak at any great length and I wish to devote myself more particularly, from this point on, to the subject that seems to be of paramount interest in connection with the budget, and that is the matter of the tariff changes. Let me say that in the remarks I have to make I have no desire to attribute to any member, or to the government, any improper motive, political or otherwise, with regard to the changes that have been made: the responsibility is theirs, I have no doubt they are acting in what they consider the best interests of Canada, but I must claim the same responsibility and the same privilege. I would also say that I have never been able to see that the determining principle as to the party with which a man should ally himself depends upon his views on the tariff. I know that is the impression of some people. I know that is the impression of some hon. gentlemen on this side; I suppose it is also the impression of some hon. members opposite. But the tariff is not the only thing with which parliament and governments have to deal. It is perhaps not even the most important thing. At any rate if my views on the tariff disentitle me to call myself a Liberal, then my life-
5 p.m. long conception of Liberalism has been incorrect.
Now, let me treat as fairly as I can the issues arising out of the budget with regard to the tariff. There are those, some of them in this House, who will not swerve from the theory of free trade but insist on carrying that principle into practice no matter what the conditions may be. They believe it is wrong to erect any tariff barrier for the purpose of giving the Canadian workman an advantage or a preference in his own country over his foreign competitor-they believe it is morally wrong and unjust to the consumer.
I think that is, perhaps, a fair description of the attitude of some members of this House. Then there are some who concede that while free trade is good in theory we should have a tariff for revenue. I believe, Mr. Speaker, there is a good deal of wrong thinking, and perhaps honest self-deception, with regard to the theory of a tariff for revenue. My contention always has been, and I still believe, that a tariff for revenue is a protective tariff. It may not be a tariff that adequately protects, as my hon. friends "angularly opposite" would say, but to the exact degree to which there is a tariff, just to that extent will the industries of Canada, or of any country, be protected. All tariffs are protective more or less.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Would my hon. friend admit that very high tariffs cease to be revenue producing?
[Mr. Euler.J

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If tariffs are high they undoubtedly are protective. If the tariff is low the element of protection exists although in very much smaller degree.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: If the tariff is too high we get no revenue.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: All those who are absolutely in theory and in practice, free traders, will say that they favour a tariff for revenue only; but if they will give the subject a moment's honest thought I think they will also say that to collect a revenue by a tariff is about as wasteful a system as can be devised and costs the country a great deal more than is commensurate with the amount that goes into the national treasury. Then there are others, like myself, who believe that it is in the national interest that we should have diversified industries. I am willing to place agriculture first and to give a prominent place to all the industries that deal with the development of our natural resources; but I will also say that manufacturing must take a very prominent part in the essential industries of Canada if we want to build up a nation with an allround development such as we ought to have. Such men believe that a tariff may be used to maintain and to encourage industry, even though sometimes it may be, apparently, at some slight sacrifice. They believe that if Canadian workmen are to be paid good wages, that will enable them to live decently and comfortably, in many lines of industry they cannot compete on an even basis with the underpaid workmen of foreign countries.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I should like the hon. member to make that clear before he goes any further. Would he mind stating plainly if he would wish the tariff to be so high that it would produce no revenue,-actually prohibit the importation of goods,-or would he define what one might call an adequate tariff that produces so much revenue and is also a protective tariff?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If the hon. member will bear with me for a moment, he will have his question answered, but I may say now that I am emphatically not in favour of a prohibitive tariff.
M. FORKE:	I should be glad to know
where the hon. member would begin and where he would end.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend desire me to go over the whole list of articles manufactured in this and every other country and say that the duty should be 15 per cent here, 20 per cent there and 30 per cent elsewhere?
I am not able to do that, and I am going ti

The Budget-Mr. Evler
give the remedy for the sort of thing which,
I think, we are suffering from if hon. -members will bear with me for a moment.
There are those of us who believe that we cannot compete on an even basis with those European countries which have lower costs of labour, whose people have a lower standard of living, whose currency is depreciated. More than that, I will include the United States with its mass production which has already been spoken of in this House to-day and its overproduction and the resulting attempts at dumping in Canada which are sometimes made. There are men-and I am one of them -who believe in a moderate tariff that will maintain Canadian industry. I believe in that as a wise policy. If that makes me a protectionist then I shall have to accept the designation. But I will also say that I do not particularly like the word "protection". In its original meaning it is beneficent and benevolent in its significance, but it has been so abused that it has acquired something of a sinister meaning. It too often connotes such a high tariff as robs the consumer, and it implies too often such a degree of protection, if you like, that it covers inefficiency in manufacture. That has been attributed to it.
I am not saying that that is true,-it is probably true in some instances-but for that reason I say that I do not particularly like the word "protection." I would just as soon speak of a tariff that maintains industry,. not a prohibitive tariff.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: An adequate tariff.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I do not usually permit words to be put into my mouth, but I am quite willing to accept the correction or the suggestion of the leader of the Progressive party. I do not favour a prohibitive tariff, but I believe in a tariff that will enable legitimate industries to live if they are efficiently conducted. I believe in that sort of a tariff also for another reason, namely, that it will give employment to our people.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Will the hon. member define "legitimate industry"?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Probably the hon. member has just as easy access to a dictionary as I have and I will leave him to find out for himself. I will draw attention, as so often has been done, to the fact that the rest of the world has erected practically prohibitive tariff walls against Canada, and unless and until that situation changes, fairplay and some degree of national self-respect as well as the desire of self-preservation dictate that we should have such a tariff as will at least
give some portion of the Canadian market to our own people. Despite text-book theories and, perhaps, I might even say text-book theorists who go back hundreds of years for their authority, that seems to me to be absolutely a reasonable position for a Canadian to take. I believe that the Laurier-Fielding tariff in its day was a reasonable tariff. Call it what you like; call it "tariff for revenue," if you wish; it was protective in its effects and under it this country was more prosperous than it had ever been before or has ever been since. I might make a- reference to the election of 1921, in connection with the tariff. The tariff was not an issue in that election in Ontario, and I think I may say in Quebec, unless it was in the constituency of the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) who, I am sorry, is not in his seat to-day.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What was the issue?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The issue was the Union government. There were two reasons why the tariff was not an issue in Ontario and Quebec. I have given one. The chief reason was that the people of this country, rightly or wrongly, and I think rightly, had decided that they were going to dispense with the government that was then in power. That was, I believe, the compelling reason throughout Canada. The second reason why the tariff was not an issue in Ontario, at least, was this, that the people of that province had confidence that the hon. gentleman, who is now Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and who had been Minister of Finance under Sir Wilfrid Laurier during a period of prosperity covering fifteen years, would again become Minister of Finance, and they had no particular fear that industry would be interfered with under his administration any more than it had been under his previous administration. But I did discuss the tariff in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and I declared myself in favour of a tariff such as I have described. The hon. member for South Winnipeg (Mr. Hudson) who is my deskmate, the other day gave some figures with regard to the election, and he stated that the Conservative party polled about a million votes and that the combined Liberal and Progressive parties polled something like two million votes. I think that is approximately correct. From that he inferred that there was a tremendous majority in favour of tariff reduction. I must take issue with my hon. friend on that. The vote of 1921, at least as regards Ontario and Quebec, was not a vote on the tariff at all, and I am quite sure that there were literally
The Budget-Mr. Eider

thousands and tens of thousands of voters who believed in the kind of a tariff that I believe in, who voted for either Liberal or Progressive candidates. In fact, I am almost inclined to say that if it had not been for the fact that the people of Ontario and Quebec had confidence that no industry would be injured by a possible Liberal government, the government which is now in office would not be now occupying the seats of office.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What about the platform of 1919?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will come to that in a
moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: There will be no injury.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hope the hon. gentleman is correct. Some reference has been made to the statement of the Minister of Finance last year that we should have tariff stability in Canada. I agreed with that at the time. I also agree with what the Prime Minister said some days ago, that that did not imply tariff stagnation. Assuredly there is room for improvement in the tariff. It is now perhaps ten years or more since the tariff was revised, and I think it is high time that we should have an intelligent revision of the tariff; but I say this, that when the Minister of Finance made that statement regarding stability, he did not contemplate that we should have frequent radical changes that would keep the business world disturbed for any length of time.
My hope has been that the government through the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) in its budget proposals would make an announcement that we should have a tariff board or commission in this country. Such a tariff board ought to be permanent.
I see my hon. friend opposite smiling; but I do not think I am stealing the thunder of my colleague the hon. member for South Waterloo (Mr. Elliot), because it will be remembered that I made this suggestion in my address on the Speech from the Throne. A tariff board of this kind should consist, if possible, of representatives of all classes of the people, including workingmen, farmers and manufacturers, if you like; but the dominant factor in the selection of its members should in my opinion be their entire fitness for the work they would undertake.
I hey should be men of integrity who would have a strong sense of responsibility and with a real desire to render public service. And I would give to that board real power; I do not believe in a tariff board, or even a committee of the cabinet, who would go about the country trying to get information 
regarding industry and succeed very often only in getting the kind of information they desired to obtain. I say, I would give that board power to make the most exhaustive investigations into .the conditions and circumstances of industry.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Was my hon.
friend satisfied with the tariff board for the appointment of which provision was made by this House in 1912 and rejected by the Senate?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I am not very familiar with the work of that board, but I venture to say that it whs not the kind of body that could do work of the description I have suggested.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It was exactly
the same, an advisory board.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I doubt very much whether the board of which my hon. friend speaks would have done what I have in mind. I would give to the board power to go into industry, find out costs and profits, ascertain whether there was watered stock upon which dividends were being paid-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That was all
provided for.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
And would they squeeze
the water out?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, we should have to
judge that by the results. The board would find out also whether there were any combines, and generally investigate into matters of that kind. If anything of the kind were discovered then I would use the tariff as a weapon to make the industry concerned give to the consumers of the country a square deal.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Perhaps it is well at
this stage to have the fact recorded that the bill to which my hon. friend (Sir Henry Drayton) has referred, and which was defeated by the party of the hon. gentleman who is now speaking, contained all these provisions that he has enumerated.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Does the right hon. gentleman say that the bill was defeated in the Senate?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes. It was bitterly
resisted for weeks in this House by the Liberal party and finally defeated by the Liberal majority in the Senate.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have no knowledge of
that, but I am willing to accept the state-

The Budget-Mr. Eider
ment of the leader of the opposition. In any event, I have only this to say, that I do not accept responsibility for what anybody did in 1912, and' much less any responsibility for what the Senate of Canada does.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
think that the tariff commission that toured this country in 1920 had the powers he speaks of?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If they had such powers
they did not exercise them, I am sure of that. In fact, that commission never reported at all, and so far as that is concerned the exMinister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) will be able to inform the House for he was the head of it. In my opinion no Minister of Finance, no committee of the cabinet, can physically obtain the information that I have spoken of, because in too many cases they are dependent almost entirely upon the officials of their departments. And I may say, with all respect to the officials of the departments, whom I have no wish to criticise generally, that I should like to be delivered in many instances from the advice that is given by some of them; I have somewhat of a dread of the official mind. A board such as I have suggested might make tariff reductions possible; I believe that is quite within the bounds of probability. I would not hesitate either, if it were shown to be advisable, to increase the tariff if I considered it in the interests of the country. I believe there are some industries here to-day that can stand a tariff reduction, but I would not make these reductions without the accurate knowledge which only such a tariff board could give. To some extent, the tariff might thus be taken out of politics, though the board would necessarily be an advisory one, and the government would always retain full responsibility.
Unfortunately, selfishness is still the most compelling motive in human life. I made that statement once before and at that time, as also on this occasion, the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) shook his head. I hope he is right, but I am afraid he is not. There are selfish men in all walks of life, and some manufacturers are no exception. Indeed, there are some who desire to have a tariff as high as Haman's gallows, to use a hackneyed expression. But such men are their own worst enemies because invariably the extremists invite extreme action in the other direction. As I said before however I believe there could be reductions in some instances without injury to industry itself and with a good deal of benefit to the consumer.
I have given a good deal of careful thought to this budget and I appreciate many of its provisions. I believe the people of Canada approve of the reductions made in the cost of living by way of the removal or the partial removal of the sales tax and I think my hon. friends directly opposite me will believe me when I say that I should like to see anything done that could possibly and legitimately be done to assist the farming industry. I think it was a year ago that we gave them the benefit of at least a portion of the Crowsnest agreement, and I understand that all the commodities under that agreement are to be' placed on the list this year.
I hope that is the case. If anything can be done to provide lower freight rates I hope it may be possible. So far as the farmers of Ontario are concerned, and particularly in my own constituency, I am quite assured of this, that their interests are the interests of the people of the cities and of the industrial towns. That at any rate is true of my own constituency.
We hear a good deal about the home market, and the westerner does not attach very much importance to that market. Perhaps he is right inasmuch as his product is very largely exported. The same may be true in the Maritime provinces also. But the home market in Ontario for the farmer is a real thing and a thing of great value. The westerners' difficulties after all, I believe it will be conceded, have no relation to the tariff; they go much deeper. The high cost of production, high freight rates, the high tariff of the country to the south, are some of the factors that enter into the problem of the western farmer. And then there is the lack of markets in which before the war the farmers of the West sold their products. If some sort of assistance could be evolved for my Progressive friends in their farming operations I should like to examine them and afford all the assistance possible; and indeed I think I could even be prevailed upon to vote for a tariff upon oleomargarine.
We have heard a good deal about the Massey-Harris Company in connection with the reduction of ithe tariff on implements. Let me remind the House that there are dozens of smaller concerns in Ontario and Quebec that also manutfacture agricultural implements. Now, I do not believe that under the amended budget proposals the manufacturers of implements are going to be seriously injured; I think not. In fact the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) yesterday stated that the implement manufacturers would make more
The Budget-Mr. Euler

money under this budget than they did before. But let me say a word for the smaller concerns manufacturing agricultural implements.' In my riding we have a concern manufacturing threshers. Last year there was imported threshing machinery to the value of $3,366,000, and there was manufactured and sold in this country only $1,850,000 worth. So that the importations were nearly twice as great as the home-manufactured product. I do not think anyone can reasonably argue that threshing machineiy enjoys a prohibitive tariff.
I am sorry the Acting Minister of Finance is not in his seat, for I wish to point out an anomaly in connection with the removal of the sales tax on threshing machinery, to show the necessity of considering very carefully any proposed changes. A threshing outfit consists of the thresher proper, the traction engine, the wind stacker, the feeder and the drive belt. On the thresher proper the sales tax has been entirely removed; but the farmer has to pay 5 per cent on the other items that go to make up the unit. It seems to me that such an inconsistency might very well be removed.
Now, Mr. Speaker, to sum up. I would say that I cannot approve of the more, or less haphazard changes that have been made in the tariff. I agree with the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) and the member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) when they say that they do not believe in tariff discrimination. The agricultural implement industry is not, I believe, injured by the tariff proposals contained in the budget. But we are told that with the free entry of its raw materials some other of our industries will be injured. The hon. member for West Hamilton (Mr. Stewart) read a good many letters pointing that way. I hope he is wrong. But no doubt it is true that some of our manufacturing industries will be injured by the proposals contained in the budget. I do not believe that for any purpose whatever it is just to discriminate against certain industries, especially those which already have lower tariff protection than almost any others that might be named.
My chief objections to the budget are these: changes are being made without an accurate knowledge of what they may involve. We are discriminating against certain industries. I do not approve of the condition of uncertainty which the country is in for the moment. I can see no very definite principle underlying the tariff reductions, unless perhaps this is the first step in the implementing of the 1919 Liberal platform. If that is the case, I say to the government:

I believe the people should know whether [DOT]the tariff platform of 1919 is to be gone on with in the sessions to come. Some hon. gentlemen on the other side a little while ago made reference to the platform of 1919. Let me say to possible critics of my attitude on the tariff when considered in conjunction with the tariff platform of 1919, that I did not support that platform, I never endorsed it, and I have on two occasions repudiated it in this House. I do so again now. Nor did the right hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) approve of that platform, as he stated on the floor of this House last session. May I give a piece of information which will probably be of interest to hon. members; in fact it is perhaps not even known to some members on this side of the House. On the resolutions committee which framed the tariff planks in the platform of 1919 there was not one Liberal member of parliament from the great industrial province of Ontario. And yet Liberal members from Ontario, whose interests were so vitally affected, are expected to defend a platform in the making of which they had no part!
I would say again, as I have already said, that I feel no particular alarm as to the immediate disastrous effects of the budget proposals. I believe there may be some injury done, but I cannot agree with those who say that industry in going to be annihilated, that the country industrially is going to come to a standstill. I do not believe it. I think some of these statements are propaganda, uttered for the sake perphaps of making political capital and therefore to be discounted.
I do not believe the injury will be so great as some have prophesied.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it becomes my duty, after listening to a well-reasoned and temperate address by the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) to express views a good deal different from those which he holds. But I assure, you, Sir, and hon. members of the House that my convictions are just as strongly held as those of the hon. member for North Waterloo.
A good deal of the discussion on the budget has consisted of declarations of hon. members either against or in favour of the protective principle. With regard to that matter I do not intend to speak at any great length; it is not my purpose to enter into an extended discussion of the theories of free trade or of protection. Having lived a good many years not far from the international boundary I have some practical knowledge of what protection has done for this country and I have had some experience in connection with the prices of goods on the respective sides of the line. However, I believe the principle of protection to be unsound, not only economically, but also from the point of view of its effect upon the morale of the people of this country. It is evident that if we have a protective system somebody is protected and somebody else must do the protecting. If somebody benefits, somebody else has got to provide that benefit. If it is done by monetary means, as is done in the case of the tariff, something must be taken from those who do the benefiting and the reward goes to those who benefit. The effect upon those who receive the protection was emphasized only yesterday by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) who said:
The threat of the "death knell of protection" has put all our manufacturers, and many of our business men who are not manufacturers, in such a position that they are afraid to make any investments, afraid to make any expansion.
"Afraid to make investments" and afraid of expansion: that is the natural consequence of protection in this or in any other country.
Tlte Budget-Mr. Fansher

A strong, virile manhood or womanhood is never developed by depending on someone else, neither is a strong, virile industry developed which depends on some other industry for assistance or for part of its revenue. When any interference which that assistance is contemplated, those who are assisted become apprehensive; fear enters their souls, as was acknowledged in the speech of the hon. member for West Toronto yesterday. While I agree with the premises taken by that hon. gentleman, with his appeal to patriotism and his desire to build up Canada, I do not agree that only by means of a protective tariff can we hope to build up a strong, well-rounded Dominion. If I quote further from his speech I think I could show that the very policy which has been in vogue in this country for the last forty years has not made a well-rounded Dominion, but has advanced prosperity and population in perhaps half a dozen or more centres throughout the country. Asked the question yesterday as to what protection had done for this country, the hon. member replied that twenty years ago Montreal and Toronto had only a small population and that to-day they have a large population. That is a fact; Toronto has doubled its population every fifteen years since its incorporation, but if we turn to rural Ontario, which is supposed to have the benefit of the home market which protectionists say is the result of the protective system, in the last twenty years rural Ontario has lost over 20,000 of its population. Only 41 townships in rural Ontario have increased in population in the last twenty years, and in those cases it was on account of the overflow from large towns or cities. Three hundred and seventy-five townships lost in population. So that if we examine the protective system we find that it does not make for a well-rounded Dominion but rather for some well-rounded centres of population throughout the country. A country cannot prosper if one industry advances much faster than others. I believe that the great basic industry of Canada, if it were left free from the necessity of helping every other industry under the sun, would again lay the foundations of and build up this country as it did in the days of the pioneers.
Coming more directly to the budget, I believe that it is a very skilful one. It is a tax reduction budget, and because it is a tax reduction budget I am pleased with it. Everybody is pleased with a budget that reduces taxation rather than increases it, but there are various methods of reducing taxation, and from the speeches of many hon. members in

this House one would be led to believe that a good deal, if not most, of the reduction made in this budget was due to reductions in the customs tariff. However, a close examination of it will not give that impression.
In the first place we have a reduction from six to five per cent in the sales tax. Now last year there was over $101,000,000 collected from the sales tax. A reduction from six to five per cent means a reduction of about $17,000,000 in sales tax alone. Besides that, we have other reductions. We have the removal of the sales tax on agricultural implements and implements connected with the farming industry, binder twine included; second, we have exemptions of the sales tax from all articles and materials to be used in the manufacture of agricultural implements; the removal of the sales tax from sulphate spraying materials, poultry feed, cream separators, and so forth. I could go on and mention about fifteen or sixteen different classes of articles from which the sales tax is either removed or on which it is materially reduced. The closest estimate that I can make of the reduction in revenue by these special reductions and exemptions in the sales tax over and above the reduction from six to five per cent would be about $5,000,000. That brings the reduction in sales tax up to about $22,000,000.
Now we notice that the total loss in revenue anticipated by a reduction in sales tax and in the tariff proposals, as given in the budget speech, is about $24,000,000, which leaves practically only $2,000,000 of a reduction in the customs tariff. With that part of the budget I am not entirely pleased. If the reduction had been in inverse ratio, or somewhere thereabouts, it would have suited me a great deal better, and I believe also the majority of the members of this House and the rank and file throughout the country. The Liberal platform of 1919 does not mention anything about a reduction in the sales tax. It speaks of a substantial reduction of the burdens of customs taxation. It is true there was a sales tax, but I do not believe there was a sales tax to amount to anything at that time. There was a sales tax, however, when, this government came into power and this government increased it in the two former budgets; it has now taken away a portion of the sales tax in this budget, so we might say:	The King government has
given and the King government has taken away. But I do not know that we can altogether add:	Blessed be the name of the
King government.

The Budget-Mr. Fansher
The two great sources of revenue are the customs tariff and the sales tax. The customs tariff provided a revenue of about $135,000,000 last year and the sales tax $101, 000,000. We have a reduction, we are told, this year of $24,000,000, which is nearly ajl accounted for by a reduction in the sales tax. That $24,000,000 reduction represents a relief to the taxpayer, but there is very little relief in excess of that amount, because the sales taxes are pretty direct taxes. On the other hand, if that reduction of $24,000000 in revenue came entirely through the customs tariff it would give a relief to the taxpayer of this country of an amount in the neighbourhood of $100,000,000, because, as everyone realizes, while about $1 goes into the treasury through the system of customs tariff collection, about $3 or $4 goes into the pockets of those who are protected.
1 just want to quote a few figures to illustrate that statement. In the year 1921 the amount of revenue collected from the automobile industry in this country and the amount of protection afforded to that industry was in the ratio of 1 to 7 j while $1 went into the treasury, $7 was afforded in protection to the manufacturers of automobiles in this country. I do not say that the whole of that $7 was taken advantage of by the manufacturers, but according to the trade returns for that year that ratio of protection was afforded. In the agricultural implement industry the ratio was $1 of revenue to $4.50 of protection. Here are some rather startling figures in connection with the boot and shoe industry. The ratio of revenue to protection afforded in the boot and shoe industry in this country in the year 1921, according to the tradte returns for that year, was $1 of revenue to $28 of protection. In the rubber goods industry, including rubber footwear, the ratio was $1 to $13. Those are the figures you get when you take the percentages and apply them to the actual amount imported and the actual amount made and sold in Canada, and if that ratio is not observed and made use of by the manufacturing industries there is surely no ground for their claim that protection should not be lower.
I wish to speak further about the automobile industry of Canada. In other budget debates a great deal has been said concerning that industry, but in the present debate there has been little or no comment. Even the budget makes no mention of the automobile industry. Now, in the part of Ontario which I have the honour to represent, it is a well known
fact that the automobile industry is able to outbid every other industry in the labour market, and the belief is current-rightly or wrongly, but I think rightly-that in a large measure its ability to do that is assisted and strengthened by the measure of protection which it enjoys under the tariff.

In the case we are considering other manufacturers are placed in a position where they cannot compete in the labour market with manufacturers of automobiles.

Mr. Chairman, was any

Objection was taken before the Banking and Commerce committee by representatives of the Imperial Life Assurance Company of Canada and the Imperial Guarantee and Accident Insurance Company of Canada. The objection was considered, and the committee decided to grant this name for certain reasons, which I may state briefly as follows: This company has had the name "Imperial" ever since its inception, and preceding that in a provincial form under a provincial charter secured in British Columbia. It was pointed out that taking the three names as a whole, the Imperial Life Assurance Company, the Imperial Guarantee Accident Insurance Company and the Imperial Insurance Office, there would be no difficulty or conflict so far as any legal transactions were concerned; and it was also pointed out that in practice the tendency is to abbreviate and that the abbreviation for the first company was the Imperial Life, and for the second company the Imperial Guarantee and that this company's abbreviated .title will be the Imperial Office. Consequently both from the standpoint of legal transactions and of usage and practice it was decided that there could be no objection to the granting of this name.

I do not know anything
about this particular matter, but while the 123
explanation of the hon. member may be very satisfactory both from the standpoint of law and of those who are accustomed to deal with these companies, I think we should regard it from the aspect of the people generally. The very fact that the word "Imperial" is used in connection with these three companies will inevitably tend to confusion in the minds of the public. As an illustration of this, I may say that a few weeks ago an insurance company in Winnipeg whose title contained the word "West" became involved and there was a great deal of confusion in the minds of the people whether it was the Great West Insurance Company or the Northwest Insurance Company. Even this slight similarity led to confusion. Therefore I think in allowing any company to use a name which is already well known there should be the greatest possible care to see that not only those accustomed to deal with them in a legal capacity but the public generally shall be able to distinguish without any possibility of confusion between the new company and those already established and well known.

CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the
House rose at six o'clock I was dealing with the protection afforded the automobile industry in this country, and I had endeavoured to show that the protection it enjoyed had enabled it to outbid other industries in the labour market, and thereby worked a hardship to industries that were more indigenous to Canada than itself.
It is a well-known fact that in southwestern Ontario labour has been drawn from the farms to the city of Windsor and adjacent towns

by the influence of the high wages being paid in the industries centered there, particularly the automobile industry. It is also a well-known fact that immigrants brought to this country to engage as farm labourers, and who have been employed to assist the farmers throughout the summer season, have very often been induced by the high wages prevailing in the border cities to relinquish their contracts with the farmers and proceed to where those higher wages can be procured. To my mind, to assist one industry by means of a protective tariff which works hardship to another industry, by making it unable to retain its labour, is not in the best interests of the state as a whole.
Then too, as we have heard from the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler) and others, it is inconceivable how one industry can be content with low protection, while another industry which uses the same raw materials receives a great deal higher protection, and in that connection I would cite the manufacturers of agricultural implements in comparison with the manufacturers of automobiles. They both use the same material, iron and steel and wood; both employ skilled workmen who are trained in the working of iron and steel and wood; and yet one industry is assisted very considerably more than the other, the automobile industry to the extent of about 35 per cent, and the other to approximately 10 per cent. It is a well-known fact that many manufacturers complain, perhaps not openly, about the unequal opportunities afforded by an unequal tariff such as is exhibited in the comparison between these two industries. I am certain that a policy such as this, which causes a discrepancy between one industry and another in their chances to procure labour, is not in the best interests of the country as a whole, and being convinced that that is the case I would like to see a policy inaugurated by this government, which is pledged by its platform to a reduction of tariffs, and which has made a start this session to implement that pledge-[DOT] I would like to see inaugurated a policy which in the course of a few years, by bringing down a few budgets, would remove about one-third of the 35 per cent protection which is afforded the automobile industry and impose an excise tax on about one-half of the protection which was left. That would still leave them a protection of about 12 per cent, a protection which is twice the average rate of interest on bonds, twice the rate of interest on most investments.
I believe there is another reason why the automobile industry should not be protected

The Budget-Mr. Fansher
to the extent it is. It has an influence in keeping up costs in other lines of manufacture. Automobiles are a thing that will be bought by people in these days; they will go without some of the things which are more essential in order to get an automobile. We see in this city and other places people riding around in the left hand corner of a limousine costing $5,000 or more-more than the price the farmer and the industrial workers of this country pay for their homes, and yet we protect the automobile industry to over one-third the purchase price of its product.
Mr. Speaker, in the last few days in our discussion of the tariff and of its protective principle we have almost lost sight of the amendment which is before us. The amendment, to my mind, is good in itself, but in view of the fact that the government is proceeding in a direction which hitherto they have been very reluctant to take, or in the words of the Speech from the Throne, being persuaded that a tariff reduction is now all that is required to bring about better conditions, I think the mover of the amendment is rather like the boy and the filbert. He wishes to have all at once, and through desiring too much may not succeed in getting any. At least, that is what might appear on a first examination of the amendment, but to my mind it is a substitute for what is already proposed, because its express wording is that all the words after " that," which is the first word in the motion for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means, be struck out and the amendment substituted therefor. For my part I believe that a bird in the hand is better than a bird in the bush.

speechtext: Or two?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I would not say there
were two birds in the amendment. I do not believe in grasping at the shadow and dropping the substance which is in sight.
Reverting to that phrase in the Speech from the Throne which represents the government as being persuaded that taxation reduction is now essential, I am afraid the government has not been persuaded exactly along the right line; the persuasion has been too much along the line of sales tax reduction and not enough in the direction of a reduction in the customs tariff. I must express my belief at this time, also, that the sales tax, which is a more direct means of raising revenue, should not be lowered to any appreciable extent in the future. The line to be followed in granting relief to the taxpayers of this country should lead to the reduction of the customs tariff. As I said earlier in my address I be-123i
lieve that the loss of. one dollar of revenue through reduction of the customs tariff will represent a gain of at least three times as much in relief to the taxpayer.
Before I conclude I wish to allude to the remark in the speech delivered yesterday by the member for West Toronto (Mr. Hocken) when referring to hon. gentlemen in this section of the chamber, he said:
I said before, Mr. Speaker, and I repeat now, that if our friends in western Canada have sufficient patriotism and are willing to assist in making Canada the great country it is capable of being made, the>
should accept a moderate protective tariff.
I wish to appeal to my hon. friend's patriotism in this regard and to say to him that if he will join wtih the captains of industry-whose cause he champions-and will engage in the work of building up this great nation on a more even doubletree than is now the case we shall get better results and I shall have more regard for his patriotism. The patriotism that requests of one industry only that it should pull this country out of the position it is in at the present; a patriotism which permits of interests on one side of the doubletree using only a minimum of effort whilst the industries which be at the very foundation of the prosperity of the state are given the short end of the haul is not to be commended. But the patriotism which will tackle in a right spirit the work that lies before us of making of Canada a truly great country, the patriotism which declares it will assume an even share of the work, the patriotism which will enter on a task in that manner and in that spirit, is a patriotism to be commended.
Now, for a brief allusion to the closing remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens). The hon. gentleman described his journey of a few weeks ago from the Pacific coast to the province of Ontario. He depicted the glories of the setting sun as he travelled through the pass in the Rocky mountains, but he did not mention the glories of the prairies. He spoke of seeing from the observation car of the train a settler at work in the fields of northern Ontario close to his home, whilst his companion stood in the door of the cottage with the children clustered round her My hon. friend said he could not help but admire these people and the work they were performing in nation building. Then he turned to the industrial worker in one of the large cities or towns of Ontario who had been identified with a particular industry for fifty years, and expressed his admiration for that worker also.
I wish to say to the hon. gentleman that if he too wishes to identify himself with the work of making this nation what it ought to
The Budget-Mr. Fansher

be he will haul on an even doubletree and permit the citizens and industrial workers to whom he alluded to do the same; and if he and the industrial concerns of Canada are actuated by that spirit they too will give evidence of a greater and more magnificent patriotism than was exhibited, for example, when the hon. gentleman tried to uphold a policy that makes for collecting toll from these same individuals.
In conclusion I must say that we as a nation have a great heritage and the development of that heritage is the task that lies before us. Our forefathers handed down to us as grand a heritage as ever was transferred from one generation to another. But while we may believe that the future this country is destined to achieve may be attained by different fiscal policies or different fiscal reforms I am certain the members of this House are all true, and loyal, and sincere in their desire and endeavours to make of this Canada of ours one of the grandest and best countries under the sun.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to address the House I congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the able way he has presented his budget proposals. I also congratulate the government on at last recognizing the wisdom and necessity of starting to carry out their 1919 programme. I appreciate this more because I fully realize that it is in recognition of the presence of the third group in the House, but for whose appearance this sort of budget would never have been presented.
9 p.m. The statement that will give the country the greatest hope, however, was when the Acting Minister of Finance said:
We have certain basic industries, upon the success of which depend the growth of all other industries, and the greater development of our trade.
Of these basic industries I would place agriculture in all its varied branches first. Next to agriculture I would place our forests, our minerals and our fisheries. The real National Policy is a policy that will encourage growth and development of these basic industries.
If Ministers of Finance would follow the lead of the present Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) and recognize that those are our basic industries, the country would derive new hope and have a stimulus to greater effort. If the Ministers of Finance for the last forty years had recognized which were the basic industries of this country, Canada to-day would be a far greater country than it is.
I should like to deal with a few of the orthodox suggestions that are put forward by various members in this House during the annual budget debates. One of the favourite

ideas of those hon. gentlemen who do not happen to make their living off the land, is that those who are on the land should go into mixed farming. Particularly is this advice given to those hon. members who come from the West. I should like to point out that that is going to have a very dire effect in the future upon the agriculturists of eastern Canada, and the day will come, and not many years hence, when, through the farmers of western Canada going into mixed farming, they will be found to be the greatest competitors of eastern Canadian farmers, both at home and abroad. I am pleased to see that the farmer members from eastern Canada do not hand out that advice; it comes from hon. members who are not interested in farming or who are not farmers themselves. Farmers in eastern Canada realize that western farmers will be real competitors and make things much worse for the eastern men as soon as they go into mixed farming.
A further suggestion relates to immigration which is held up as another of the cure-alls. Immigration of the right sort is what we want; volunteer immigration is all right; but immigration that is forced, as has been the case for some years past, and as was particularly the case last year, is forced at a great cost to this country. A good deal of criticism was offered from this side of the House during the immigration debate last year, because we realized that the government would be spending a great deal of money and probably throwing most of it away. What do we find is the result to-day? We find that although the government spent some $3,500,000, every single settler that was brought into Canada plus 45,000 more have gone to the United States!
Another suggestion often given out at this time is that everybody should practise rigid economy. While to practise economy individually is all right, it is a terrible weapon, if carried out on a wholesale scale, as it would then cripple commerce in every way.
Another statement often made is that labour costs are too high, and labour comes in for a good deal of condemnation. I should like to put on record a few figures with regard to labour costs, in order to show that, when all is said and done, labour costs are not always the greatest costs with which we have to contend. I should like to give an example to show how labour costs are often small, comparatively speaking, in comparison with other charges. In a statement given by Sir Adam Beck, in referring to the Hydro-Electric Commission, he gave these figures:
Estimated revenue from power plant for 1924, $9,500,000.

The Budget-Mr. Spencer
This would be distributed as follows:
Interest	$ 6,200,000
Sinking fund	 1,217,000
Depreciation	 410.000
Operation	 1,280,000	$9,107,000
Surplus for the year..	$ 393,000
Or a surplus for the year of nearly $400,000.
While listening to the debates in this House, it has often occurred to me how contradictory certain statements are. For instance, hon. members who sit to my right have for two [years been continually criticising the government for not carrying out their pledges. This year because the government are attempting to carry out their pledges-and we should give them credit for that-we find they are receiving just as harsh criticism from the Conservatives for trying to do so.
Another contradiction which I might point out is this. Regarding the group to which I have the honour to belong, representing, as it mainly does, the agricultural constituencies of western and eastern Canada, the farmers have often been criticised for not getting down to business and organising. Now that they have organized and sent some sixty odd members to this House, their action seems to be criticised and not at all well received.
We have heard a good deal lately during this debate of the way in which the people are leaving the country because of this low tariff budget. That argument, from my Conservative friends at my right might hold water if it were not for the fact that for some years past while we had what might be called a reasonably high tariff we lost very large numbers.
Further advice given to the farmers is such as this:	They are told to work harder, to
produce more and to be thrifty. As one who knows the life of the farmer very intimately, I should like to know how farmers can be expected to work much harder. As regards producing more, I think they have done their share in that respect, and as regards being thrifty, it is hard to tell how the majority of the fanners could be more thrifty than they are. It is rather amusing when you consider the criticisms that are brought against the orientals who are coming into this country and the reasons given why certain people do not want them to be kept in Canada. The reasons given, are that they work too hard, they produce too much and they are too thrifty.
For some years past, indeed, I may say for many years, through what you might call class legislation, the basic industries of this country have had very little attention paid
to them, with the result that they have suffered very much, and to-day are at a particularly low ebb, so low that you find that the agricultural people are able to pay a very small percentage, according to their numbers, as their part of the income tax bill of this country. Then the criticism is made of these people. "Why don't they pay income tax"?
We also hear a good deal in regard to the present standard of living in Canada, which it is said, should be higher. At the same time we find large sums of money being spent on immigration literature in central Europe with the idea of bringing a lot of those people out here, officials must be perfectly well aware that if any large numbers of these people are introduced into the country the standard of living is apt to be lowered. For some years past it has always been the aim of the Minister of Immigration with his staff to encourage people coming to this coutry to take up farming, and for a while no one was encouraged to come unless he settled on the land. I believe the doors are thrown open a little wider to-day, but one point which the Minister of Immigration should realize quite fully is this, that you cannot force people to farm, irrespective of conditions. If economic conditions are unjust, uneven, unequal, or unfair, you cannot force people tc farm, and if you succeed in getting them to go on the land they will not settle down under these conditions. We are making great efforts to curtail unemployment, but at the same time by this system of immigration, whereby we have induced people to come to the country' out of proportion to the demands of industry, we naturally swell the ranks of the unemployed annually.
From the year 1911 onwards hon. gentlemen to my right-Conservatives-have done their level best to frustrate any chances we may have had of securing reciprocity with the United States, so that through their action we lost the best stock market we could have had. And now that we have lost that market we are told by these same gentlemen that we should go in for mixed farming. We have heard a good deal about the supposed agreement between the party representing the government and those gentlemen amongst whom I happen to sit. Criticisms have been made of a close alliance which it is alleged exists between these two groups. Well, Mr. Speaker, it is interesting, on consulting Hansard, to find that in the year 1923, of 21 votes that were taken, in 12 the Liberals and Conservatives voted together against the Progressives, on four occasions the Liberals and
