speechtext: It is understood, Mr. Speaker, that we are to go on with Supply-Agriculture.
The House in Committee of Supply, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
M:r. Chairman, I have
been requested by one or two hon. gentlemen to let vote 46 stand for the present. We will proceed with vote 47.
Agriculture publications, $33,500.

The extra amount
is for publicity and bulletins for distribution during the Empire Exhibition this summer.

Item agreed to.
International Institute of Agriculture, $15,000.
Of what value is this?

We decided not
to send delegates to Rome in connection with the institute this year, the idea being to economize as much as possible. We are keeping up our dues in the usual way and maintaining the staff here.

Will the minister explain
what benefit Canada gets from that?

Agricultural statistics of the world are compiled by a body located at Rome, representing some 62 countries. The information is assembled there from month to month and redistributed to the various countries concerned. Farmers and others interested are thus made familiar with the amount of grain and 'other products
Supply-A gricidture

produced in the various countries, and if, for instance, there is a surplus in any particular line, those interested in growing that product may regulate their sowing accordingly. I do not think the average farmer pays very much attention to that side of it. It is largely a matter of the securing of information of a statistical nature for governments, individuals and the press. For instance, last year we discovered through the medium of this body that Canada had become the largest grower of export wheat in the world. Of course we might have found that out a few months afterwards in any case. I do not suppose anything serious would happen if we did1 not have this institute. But we are working in co-operation with about 60 other countries, and sometimes you have to keep up your part when you are in an institute of this nature, even though you may not be able to point to any very outstanding results from it. I do not think we would care to retire from our connection with the institute.

What is the basis of
contribution? Do we pay as much as the United States, say, or is it on a per capita basis?

The countries are
classified into groups. The United States this year are sending over something like 23 representatives; they are making a feature of it. There is a contribution to the expenses of Sir Thomas Elliott, located at Rome, who is delegate for Canada and Great Britain on the permanent committee. The countries are grouped according to importance and a levy is made for the maintenance of the office in Rome and the distribution of the information as it comes in. The home offices are maintained by the respective governments.
I got some information, but it was not what I asked. What I asked was: How do we tell what we ought to contribute? Is it per capita?

The respective
countries have the option of belonging to whatever group they like. Canada elected to belong to group 2, and that involves a certain contribution, amounting to almost $7,000 for the office in Rome. The balance goes to maintain the office here in the West Block.

What does the office
in the West Block do? How does it co-operate with Rome?

They compile the
statistics at this end and transmit them to the headquarters at Rome, and then in turn they receive them back when the totals are realized there and redistributed. Mr. Doherty, who is in charge of the office here, has been engaged in that work for a number of years. They have a very substantial library. The staff numbers about five.

The whole thing is a
mystery to me. It may be all right, but I cannot understand it. The purpose is to get statistics of agricultural production. Well, why there needs to be an institute at Rome or anywhere else to do that, I do not know to begin with. We have our system of statistics, so has every country; you can find oui agricultural production any time you telephone our statistical office, and every other country has a corresponding system. There is no doubt in the world that every agricultural department or any government can get from the other governments and does get regularly the statistics of agricultural production, just as we get the statistics of manufacturing production and of railways.

It is a clearing
house.

What in the world do
we need a clearing house for? There may be need bf it, but it is not apparent to me. You might have a clearing house for every class of production on earth. I am always suspicious of these international bodies. The world is getting top-heavy with machinery.

My hon. friend
does not think it is something that I have sprung on the country, does he?

No, I do not think the
hon. gentleman sprang it on the country, but I would like to get some explanation of it that is intelligible, and I have not got it yet.
I will now come to the office here. Why should there be a sort of Canadian radio centre to get this from Rome? What is our statistics office for? They will get this information just as easily. Why a receiving station here with five or six of a staff? I am not particularly criticizing the minister, except I do not think he has gone into it very much. I do not doubt if the former minister were here he would have some defence of it.

If the hon. gentleman will sit down I will tell him something of it.

Supply-Agriculture
I hope so. I waited patiently through his last three or four efforts, but without much glimmering of the purpose of this office.
I took it for granted you knew a little bit about it to begin with.
I do not think the minister would if he had not his deputy beside him.

I cannot recall the
exact date, but I remember a gentleman by the name of David Lubin getting the notion into his head of organizing a world institute of this nature for the purpose of consolidating the statistics of the world, particularly those relating to agriculture. I was at Regina at that time, and I know the Hon. Sydney Fisher, who was then Minister of Agriculture, was one of the first delegates who went over from Canada. David Lubin is the gentleman responsible for having this notion. I cannot give my hon. friend his history, but I am sure he must have heard of him. I think a good many in the committee will recall that about that time there was a mania for collecting statistics. You heard talk of statistics everywhere, and this gentleman seemed to get the idea of wanting to go everybody else one better by getting world statistics from the various countries. Some thirty-two countries fell in line with his proposition, and the scheme crystallized in Rome where a permanent office has been established. I do not know exactly how large a staff they have, but we contribute about $7,000 towards its maintenance. Thirty countries gather their statistics at home and transmit them to Rome, and there they are consolidated and distributed all over the world. That is briefly the story of this organization. Whether it is worth this amount of money I cannot say. I have never attended one of the meetings, but some of the ministers in the past have taken the opportunity of going over and seeing for themselves. I do not expect I shall, but if I had taken the opportunity I would be in a position to give my hon. friend first-hand information on the details. I must say that I never was very much struck with the work when it was first inaugurated, but it was here when this government came into power. Our delegates who went over two years ago made a special report to me, and they seemed to think they would not by any means care to recommend that this work be dropped; they thought the institute was doing a useful work. If we were hard enough up we could do without it, but nevertheless we joined with these other countries in establishing this institute, and other countries instead of relaxing their interest seem to be
taking a deeper interest in it. The United States, for instance, instead of sending over two or three delegates is sending twenty-three this year. We are not sending any delegates this year.
Who is this supposed to benefit?

I indicated that
possibly when my hon. friend was out-the farmers and people generally who are interested in these returns.

Does the minister himself
think that the farmers derive one dollar's worth of benefit from the money that is spent on this work?

I do not think the farmers govern their actions one particle by these statistics. If there is a surplus of any particular product the farmers are supposed to be made acquainted with it and govern themselves accordingly in their sowing operations, but there is not one farmer in ten thousand who actually governs himself by this information. But that was one of the dreams of the originator. As a matter of furnishing actual information however, it is possibly worth while. We are a wheat-growing country, and the largest exporter of wheat in the world, and as I pointed out a few moments ago we were given information on the wheat situation through this medium, and that is_ only one illustration of the useful information that has come to us through this medium. We got along before this institute was Qrganized, but then, of course, we got along without many other things too prior to that, and for my part I would not like to see us drop out of it without consultation with the various countries with whom we co-operated in the first instance.

Through what channels
does this information reach the people it is supposed to benefit?

Through press
despatches, the agricultural press particularly, and through bulletins. I am sure my hon. friend must have seen Mr. Doherty's articles from time to time.

They issue a very elaborate report. It has been coming to me for . some years, but I cannot say just how often it comes because I do not read it very carefully. They send this report around to some people; I do not know to whom.

Is Canada committed
in any way with the other nations to keep up this establishment in Rome?
Suppl y-A (jricidture

The contract just
coninues from year to year. The United States got into correspondence with us and their delegates offered to convene with ours here and go over together, bu't we were obliged to tell them we were not sending delegates this year. They went ahead with their own plans and are sending twenty-three delegates this year, so as far as this continent is concerned the United States figured that we would remain in the institute at least until we gave notification to the contrary. There is no contract signed to stay in with it for any length of time, but it just goes on from year to year. At the same time it is supposed to be a progressive movement so far as statistics are concerned, and when other countries are going into it so strong as the United States, for instance, it would not look a very good time for us to do anything else than remain in it.

Do I understand
my hon. friend to suggest that this year we should carry along with the organization, and in the meantime notify the other countries that we contemplate withdrawing before another year?

If we cannot withdraw at once, if we are bound to give a year's notice, we must observe that obligation with the understanding that we reserve the right to withdraw next year. But I understood we could withdraw at once.

It is the central [DOT]
body at Rome that we are committed to, but various countries are co-partners in the enterprise. The institute was established with the understanding, of course, that the expense would be borne by the various countries that are getting the service which it supplies. I

think in ordinary common decency we should give notice of reasonable time in advance before w" withdrew from the arrangement. I may say that two years ago when we were sending a representative over to a conference at Rome I asked for a candid report as to the value of this work to Canada. The report I received was not very pronounced either orre way or the other but the general tone of it was that we had better continue the arrangement. Personally I think we could dispense with it to-day and we would not know to-morrow that we had lost anything very substantial. At the same time I have never been at a world conference of this nature and am only able to speak from secondhand information. Consequently I do not know what my judgment would be if I saw the conference in operation. Apparently it is just one of those things that grew out of the prosperity of former days, and ran along, and a great many people think it is all right. 1 have never heard any other country discuss it. I was the only adverse critic-at least the only "doubting Thomas"-that I knew of in Canada two or three years ago. I made inquiry and was told it was a fine institution and I had to put, and did put, my opinion to one side. I think in many respects it is of no practical value to the farmer in guiding his farming operation on the land.
In view of the strong statement the minister has just made I would ask him if he would take into consideration the withdrawal of this item for next year at least?

I will recommend it to my colleagues. We have international relationships with other countries in this matter, and we would have to look into it very carefully-I am not supposed to knock the matter out right off my own bat. However, I will tell my hon. friend this: I will recommend to my colleagues that I think we can dispense with it. I may say that I have already done that, as a matter of fact.
What is the total cost of keeping this office up? Do the various countries-twenty-eight I think the minister said-bear the expense equally?
What is the total cost of all the countries?

Yes, the cost of maintaining
this office in Rome?

Well, it will be
more than thirty times seven.

Supply-A griculture

I just multiplied $15,000, which is the item, by twenty-eight-I thought from what the minister said there were twenty-eight countries concerned-and I see it comes to $428,000. I was wondering what sort of office it would be to cost that much money. It would' have to be a very extensive one certainly. Now, do the countries concerned all bear an equal share, or how is the expense provided for?

I am just figuring
out how much it will be. I went over that once and I am sorry my hon. friend was not in when I gave an explanation previously. The cost is about $210,000 assuming they all pay about the same as Canada, but I imagine a lot of them would pay quite a bit more. We are in number two group, number one group would be more expensive.

I was asking the minister
on what basis we contribute? I suppose we do not "go it blind." There is some basis on which Canada is asked to contribute a certain amount of money, and I presume there is something to show why we are asked to put up $15,000?

I have gone over
that already. The countries are divided into three groups-one, two and three. An estimate is made of ,the amount for the total requirements and it is allocated to the various countries in these three groups. It is an arbitrary amount to suit the sum that has to be allocated. We had the option of choosing what group we would go into and we went into group number two.

The whole of the vote
does not go to the central office in Rome. According to the details of expenditure for
1922-	23 out of practically $15,000 expended, only $2,754 was contributed to the central institute in Rome. Now, would the minister be good enough to tell us how much of last year's vote was really expended in the year
1923-	24?

I have not been
able, perhaps, to catch the entire significance of my hon. friend's question but if my conception of what he has asked is correct I will give my explanation if he will be seated just for a moment. The amount that we send over every year is not always the same. Sofnetimes we are behind with our contribution. If we are a little short in the vote sometimes we get a year behind, and the next year we require that much more.
Oh, oh.

Hon. gentlemen
opposite seem to be amused, it is all right.

I will make my question
sufficiently intelligible to the minister this time. During the year 1922-23 the International Institute of Agriculture cost this country $14,269. Of that amount $2,754 was the contribution *to the institute at Rome for 1922, I presume-I think I am right-that the contribution for 1923 will be something on a par with the contribution for 1922.
No.

Hence I say that out of
that vote of practically $15,000 two years ago, something like $2,750 was expended for the central institute in Rome. The balance went for stationery, advertising, printing, publication and the expenses of the delegates representing this Dominion at Rome?
Cigars and cigarettes.

I feel a good deal like
an hon. gentleman who sits to my left, who said we could easily dispense with this item. The minister himself said that he had been "a doubting Thomas" and he has not as yet confessed1 that he is confirmed in his belief that this is a necessity. He has admitted to us that no one interested in the farming industry of this country has reaped or will reap one cent's worth from this expenditure. I take into consideration the fact that in the interest of economy the federal vote to the different provinces in connection with agricultural instruction has been curtailed, and I think we might as well curtail this item also.

I am not sure the hon. gentleman is entirely right; I think the minister has distributed his opinions very fairly. He said this vote could be dispensed with and that nobody ever benefits from it at all, that there is no value in it. He also said that it is a fine institute. He further said that he is ready to propose to his colleagues to have nothing more to do with it. I do not think we could ask for a finer variety of opinions than that. May I ask last of all if Mr. Marshall had a trip over there to this institute? Has he been one of the delegates yet?

No. My hon.
friend has a great faculty of presenting a thing so as to make it appear exactly what it is not. I said that so far as it was an advantage to the farmer, its advantage was not appreciable; and that, as a matter of
Suppl y-A gricidture

fact, I did not think it was of any value as regards determining his course of conduct in sowing his fields to fit in with the reports of the institute. I did not think it had any effect in that regard at all. That was one of the dreams and theories of David Lubin; that was one of the advantages which he preached in order to get the various countries to take this up. But from an international standpoint, surely sixty countries that are engaged in this work are not all so foolish as to throw money away just to give a few people a trip to Rome. We have joined with these countries; we have committed ourselves to support the central office at Rome, and if we desire to retire from it, I think we should notify the central office a year in advance. It is quite correct that it will not cause me very much grief to notify them, but in the meantime I would not want to retire from this institute until we had given the ordinary business intimation that we were going to do so and had observed the ordinary proprieties between countries.

I am sorry to find
the minister retiring from the position which he assumed two years ago and a year ago. When he came into office, an amount of $10,000 was voted for this object. The International Institute of Agriculture at Rome was a new venture at that time, when he saw fit to increase the expenditure by $5,000 and the following year by another $5,000, really doubling the expenditure from the time he came into office. To-day he tells us that he is a "doubting Thomas," and he doubts whether we are receiving any benefit from this expenditure or not. If we are not receiving any benefit, I do not think we have any money to throw away. He says that all we have ascertained is that Canada is the greatest wheat exporting country in the world. The institute is an international agricultural intelligence bureau for the collection, elaboration and publication of technical, practical, economic and statistical information of interest to agriculturists, special prominence being given to crop reports, prices, visible supply, imports and exports, methods of cultivation, agricultural chemistry and botany, plant breeding, plant diseases, meteorology, forestry, live stock, agricultural industries, co-operation, insurance, credit, agricultural organization and administration.
The matter of co-operative activities was the primary thing that David Lubin had in mind, because he was a strong advocate of co-operation.
The institute publishes three regular bulletins:
(a)	International Review of the Science and Practice of Agriculture, which might be called a review of reviews of agriculture, its material being abstracted from some 2,600 periodicals from all countries and in many languages.
(b)	International Review of Agricultural Economics, which deals with co-operation, credit, farm management, and other economic questions relating to agriculture.
(c)	International Crop Report and Agricultural Statistics, which contains official reports of crop conditions and estimates of the area and production of all important crops, as well as statistics of international trade, prices of agricultural products, numbers of live stock, etc. Yearly statements of the production of and trade in fertilizers and concentrated feeding stuffs are published.
